title: Cardiac Plasticity in Aquaculture: Influence of Aquaculture Practices on Heart Morphology and Performance in Fish
content:
ABSTRACT

Aquaculture has profoundly shaped the genetics of farmed fish while subjecting them to environmental conditions that diverge significantly from their wild equivalents. As a key driver of physiological plasticity in fish, the shifts in physiological and environmental demands associated with aquaculture can induce cardiac remodeling, resulting in changes to heart morphology and performance. This review discusses the existing knowledge on heart remodeling in finfish aquaculture and its importance for fish performance. Here, we described the morphological deviations in size, form, and structure of the hearts of farmed fish relative to their wild conspecifics that were statistically supported by meta-analysis, including a general rounding of the heart and alterations in its symmetry, especially for salmonid species. To get to the heart of these cardiac alterations, we also reviewed how aquaculture practices, focusing on factors related to genetics, environmental conditions, nutrition, disease, and stress, have changed the cardiac morphology of farmed fish. When looking into implications on cardiac performance, the aquaculture-induced cardiac plasticity seems either beneficial or pathological. Overall, this review highlights the propensity of aquaculture practices to cause changes in heart morphology, but understanding the functional consequences and underlying mechanisms of these alterations necessitates comprehensive, integrated research that considers the intricate interactions among genetic, environmental, and physiological influences.
